params.text:
The law behind speaking up

The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (PIDA) gives legal protection to workers who blow the whistle. It does not protect every complaint — it protects a “qualifying disclosure”, which becomes a protected disclosure when it is made in the right way. To be protected, you must:

  • disclose information you reasonably believe shows a qualifying wrongdoing (you do not have to be proved right — an honest, reasonable belief is enough); and
  • reasonably believe the disclosure is in the public interest — about protecting others, not settling a personal grievance; and
  • raise it through an appropriate route, such as your employer or a prescribed person.

These are “day one” rights — you are covered from your very first day at work, with no minimum length of service required.

Categories of qualifying wrongdoing

PIDA sets out the types of wrongdoing that a protected disclosure can be about. Your concern should fit one of these categories:

  • A criminal offence — for example theft, fraud or physical assault.
  • A breach of a legal obligation — failing to meet a duty set out in law or regulation.
  • A danger to health and safety of any person.
  • A miscarriage of justice.
  • Damage to the environment.
  • The deliberate concealment (cover-up) of any of the above.

In social care, abuse and neglect will usually fall within a criminal offence, a breach of a legal obligation, or a danger to health and safety.

Good faith and tiers of disclosure

Since the law was updated in 2013 you no longer have to prove you acted in “good faith”, though acting honestly still matters and bad faith can reduce any award you might receive. The law also recognises tiers of disclosure:

  • To your employer: usually the first and easiest step.
  • To a prescribed person: a named body such as the CQC.
  • Wider disclosure: for example to the media, allowed only in limited and stricter circumstances.

params.taskDescription: Complete the summary of what makes a disclosure protected under PIDA.
params.textField: A protected disclosure must be about a *qualifying* wrongdoing. The worker only needs a *reasonable* belief that the information is true, and must believe the disclosure is in the *public* interest. Protection applies from the worker's first *day*, with no minimum length of *service* required.

params.question: Under PIDA, when does a concern become a “protected disclosure”?

answers.text: When you have a reasonable belief it shows serious wrongdoing and you raise it in the public interest through the right channel.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Reasonable belief, a public-interest purpose and the right route together make a disclosure protected.

answers.text: Only when you can prove the wrongdoing beyond doubt before you report it.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. You need a reasonable belief, not cast-iron proof; investigating is not your job.

answers.text: Only if you report it straight to the media so the public hears about it.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Wider disclosure to the media is only protected in limited circumstances; usually you start with your employer or a prescribed person.

answers.text: Automatically, whenever you complain about anything at work.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A personal grievance is not the same as a public-interest disclosure about serious wrongdoing.
